body:
Shabbos Chazon: Rebuke as a Tool for Rebuilding

Tochachah · Emes · Success · Vision

I. Moshe's Last Will and Testament

Shabbos Devarim is also Shabbos Chazon, and Sefer Devarim carries a particular personal weight. It was the first sefer completed in its entirety when this journey of weekly Divrei Torah began, and it has held a special place ever since.

Rabbi Yehoshua Gordon, zichrono livrachah, used to describe Sefer Devarim as Moshe Rabbeinu's last will and testament. That is exactly what it is. These are the final weeks of Moshe's life, and this is how he chooses to spend them: standing before Klal Yisrael and speaking. Not performing miracles. Not issuing new commandments. Speaking. Giving tochachah. Reminding the nation of everything that went wrong during the forty years in the desert, the Eigel, the complaints, the sin of the meraglim, the failures and the stumbling blocks.

Which raises an obvious question. This is Moshe's final opportunity to address the people he has led for forty years. The next generation stands ready to enter Eretz Yisrael. What would we expect from this moment? Encouragement, perhaps. A vision of what lies ahead. Instead, Moshe spends much of Sefer Devarim reviewing what went wrong.

Why?

II. A Great-Grandfather's Last Honesty

There is a mashal of a great-grandfather approaching one hundred and twenty years, surrounded by children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and perhaps great-great-grandchildren. Of course he shares words of blessing and encouragement. But he also has one final opportunity to be honest. He can say: I know how much potential you have. I know how much good you can accomplish. But before I leave, let me remind you of the stumbling blocks that can get in your way, because I may not be here to remind you later.

We see something similar with Yaakov Avinu before his passing. Alongside the blessings there are corrections and warnings. There is love, but there is also what we might call tough love. That is much of what Sefer Devarim is about. Growth. Alignment. Refinement. Remembering who we were so we can become who we are meant to be.

It is also worth noting who Moshe is actually speaking to. These are not the people who left Mitzrayim. That generation carried a slave mentality, and despite witnessing open miracles at every turn, they stumbled repeatedly. Chazal teach they would not be the ones to enter the land. The generation Moshe addresses in Sefer Devarim is their children, and they had a very different reality ahead of them.

These children had grown up with the mann. They had never needed to work for food. Now they were about to enter a world where they would place a seed into the ground, watch it decay, and see grain emerge. They would plow, plant, harvest, and bake bread. Hashem was bringing them to a level where they would become partners in creation. That is a dignity and a responsibility that this generation had to understand before they crossed the Yarden. Moshe's tochachah was not punishment. It was preparation.

III. How Many Truths Exist?

This week, Rav Channen posed a question to our chavurah: how many truths exist in the world?

The easy answer, the one that sounds thoughtful and open-minded, is that everyone has their own truth based on their experiences and their perspective. But that is not actually true. There may be many ways to understand and approach truth. There may be many angles from which truth can be seen. But truth itself is singular. Hashem is emes. Torah is emes. When truth gets filtered through a personal lens, distorted by desires or fears or prior assumptions, it becomes something else. It may feel true. But it is not necessarily emes.

Rav Channen also said something else that stayed with me. Hashem wants us to succeed. Hashem gives us all the tools we need to succeed. The respectful pushback was this: before we can discuss success, we first need to define it. Success according to whom? According to my own picture of what my life should look like? Or according to Hashem's ratzon?

Rav Gerzi of Pilzno speaks often about refining our middos until our will aligns with Hashem's will. The Avos were successful because their definition of success was identical to Hashem's definition of success. That changes how we view everything. People ask why bad things happen to good people. From our limited perspective they appear bad. From the perspective of emes, Hashem's emes, they are part of a greater good we do not yet fully understand.

IV. Moshe's Definition of Success

Approaching Sefer Devarim through that lens, Moshe Rabbeinu's words take on an entirely different quality. Moshe was the greatest navi who ever lived. His ratzon was aligned with Hashem's ratzon to a degree no other human being has achieved. Even when he forgot a halachah, he never experienced it as personal failure. He understood that someone else was meant to bring that particular teaching forward, that there was a reason for the gap.

Moshe understood that every challenge, every difficulty, and every apparent disappointment was part of Hashem's plan. Even at the very end of his life, when he is told that he will see Eretz Yisrael but not enter it, he accepts the decree. Why? Because his definition of success was never entering the land. His definition of success was fulfilling Hashem's will. And that he had done.

The tochachah of Sefer Devarim is not Moshe venting his frustrations before he dies. It is Moshe giving the next generation the most honest gift he can offer: a clear-eyed account of what went wrong and why, so that they might avoid those same stumbling blocks as they build what comes next.

V. Chazon: Vision and the One Who Helps Others Hear

The Haftorah of this Shabbos gives us the word Chazon, which means vision. The Navi Yeshayahu opens with a prophetic vision, and much of what follows is difficult to hear. We are entering the Nine Days. Tishah B'Av is approaching. The words of the haftorah speak of a relationship that was neglected, of a nation that turned away from Hashem after everything He did for them.

But the word Chazon shares a root with chazzan, the one who leads the congregation in tefillah and helps others listen and connect. A chazzan does not sing for himself. He sings to draw others into the prayer, to help them hear what they might not reach on their own. There is something in that connection worth sitting with. The vision of Shabbos Chazon, as painful as it can feel, is not delivered to crush. It is delivered to draw us in. To help us hear what we might otherwise avoid. To help us see where we are and where we could be.

VI. The Muscle Fiber Mashal

There is a helpful way to understand what tochachah actually does to a person. When someone exercises and builds strength, what is actually happening in the body is the opposite of what it looks like from the outside. The muscle fibers are being torn apart. They are being broken down. And if the person then provides the body with what it needs, protein, proper nutrition, rest, those fibers rebuild stronger than they were before. The breakdown was not the goal. The goal was the rebuilt strength that followed.

Tochachah works the same way. Without the proper ingredients, rebuke feels only painful. With the proper ingredients, humility, emunah, honesty, and a genuine desire to grow, the rebuke becomes one of the most powerful tools for transformation available to us. The words may sound difficult. But they are actually building material. That is what Moshe Rabbeinu is giving us in Sefer Devarim. That is what the haftorah is giving us. That is what Shabbos Chazon is giving us.

VII. What We Are Building

Chazal teach that every generation in which the Beis HaMikdash is not rebuilt is considered as though it was destroyed in that generation. That teaching is not meant to weigh us down with inherited guilt. It is meant to remind us that what we do today matters. At the same time, we also learn that each of us is meant to be a Mishkan for the Divine Presence. We are building ourselves. We are the vessel.

Perhaps that is the deepest message of Shabbos Chazon. The visions and warnings and reminders we encounter this week do not need to remain painful memories of what once was. With the right ingredients, with humility and emunah and a willingness to be honest about where we are, they can become the tools through which we build what will be. May we merit to see the rebuilding of the Beis HaMikdash speedily in our days, and may the vision of this Shabbos become a vision of that future rather than only a memory of the past.

חזק ואחזק

Good Shabbos

Reflection Questions

• Whose definition of success am I actually using? When I evaluate whether my life is going well, am I measuring against Hashem's ratzon or against my own picture of what things should look like?

• When I receive tochachah, whether from a teacher, a family member, or my own conscience, do I hear it as an attack or as building material? What determines which way it lands?

• Like Moshe being told he would see but not enter Eretz Yisrael, is there something I have accepted, or need to accept, as part of Hashem's plan even though it is not what I would have chosen?

• The generation entering Eretz Yisrael was about to become partners in creation through the dignity of work. Where in my own life have I lost sight of that dignity, either by avoiding real effort or by forgetting what the effort is ultimately for?

• Chazon means vision. What is the vision I am carrying for my own life and for Klal Yisrael right now? Is it informed by emes, or is it filtered through my own distortions and preferences?

• What are the ingredients I need right now for tochachah to rebuild me rather than simply hurt me? Which of those am I currently missing?
